nameStory: Admestina tibialis gets its scientific name from its distinctive tibiae - the fourth segment of each leg that often shows unique characteristics in jumping spiders. The genus name Admestina comes from classical origins, though this little jumper is more focused on hunting than ancient history. Like many jumping spiders, it lacks a widely-used common name, so spider enthusiasts simply call it by its scientific name.
description: Admestina tibialis is a small jumping spider that belongs to the incredibly athletic family of hunters known for their excellent vision and impressive leaping abilities. These compact spiders are tiny enough to sit comfortably on your fingernail, typically measuring just a few millimeters in body length. Instead of spinning webs to catch prey, they actively hunt other small insects and spiders, stalking them like miniature cats before pouncing with remarkable precision. With their forward-facing eyes and alert posture, they're among the most engaging spiders to observe.

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Four large forward-facing eyes arranged in a row across the front of the head, giving it an almost cute, inquisitive expression - like tiny black beads that seem to watch you back

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, robust build with a relatively flat profile and slightly fuzzy texture, similar to velvet when viewed up close

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in quick, jerky motions with frequent stops to assess surroundings, often raising front legs and turning to face observers directly

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Tiny spider, small enough to easily fit on a dime with room to spare, making it easy to overlook despite its bold hunting behavior

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates no hunting web, but spins small silk retreats under bark or in crevices that feel like finding a miniature sleeping bag

habitat: Look for Admestina tibialis in diverse habitats across New England, from forest floors to rocky outcrops where they hunt among leaf litter and low vegetation. They're particularly fond of areas with good sun exposure where they can warm themselves on rocks or bark surfaces. Given the single observation record in New England, they're likely quite rare or easily overlooked in our region.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, emerging from winter hiding spots to hunt and begin mating behaviors.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible hunting during warm, sunny days and females may be carrying egg sacs.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues but begins to slow as spiders prepare for winter, with young spiders dispersing from summer egg sacs.
seasonality.winter: Overwinter as juveniles or adults in protected locations under bark, rocks, or deep in leaf litter.

funFact: Jumping spiders like Admestina tibialis can see in color and have vision comparable to a cat's - they can spot and track prey from distances up to 20 times their own body length, making them incredible tiny predators with eyesight that puts most spiders to shame.
confusionNotes: With only one confirmed observation in New England, Admestina tibialis could easily be confused with other small jumping spiders in the region. The key difference is in the specific arrangement and size of those forward-facing eyes, though distinguishing between tiny jumping spider species often requires expert examination.
contextualKnowledge: The extremely low observation count (just one record) in New England suggests this species is either at the very edge of its range here, incredibly secretive, or possibly represents a misidentification or unusual occurrence - making any sighting potentially significant for regional spider records.
compareHints: Admestina tibialis differs from its relative A. wheeleri primarily in subtle leg and body proportions that require microscopic examination to distinguish reliably. Compared to other jumping spiders in New England, Admestina species are generally smaller and more secretive than the common bold jumpers or zebra spiders you're likely to encounter. Their behavior is similar to other jumping spiders, but their tiny size and rarity make them a special find.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The thick-legged jumping spider differs from its close relative, the thin-legged jumping spider (Admestina tibialis), primarily in its more robust leg structure and stockier overall build.
